nameStory: The humpback whale gets its name from the distinctive hump on its back that becomes prominent when the whale arches to dive deep. This curved silhouette, combined with their habit of rolling through the water in a humped motion, made early whalers think of a hunched back. The scientific name Megaptera means 'big wing,' referring to their incredibly long pectoral fins that can stretch up to one-third of their body length.
description: Humpback whales are massive marine mammals that can reach 46-56 feet long and weigh up to 44 tons - imagine a school bus that weighs as much as 22 cars! They have a distinctive body shape with extraordinarily long pectoral fins, bumpy tubercles covering their enormous heads, and deeply grooved throats. These gentle giants are famous for their acrobatic breaching behavior, launching their entire bodies out of the water in spectacular displays that thrill whale watchers. Male humpbacks also produce hauntingly beautiful songs that can last up to 33 minutes.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Massive whale 46-56 feet long with a distinctive humped back when diving. The head is broad and covered in knobby bumps called tubercles that feel like giant warts, each sprouting bristly hairs.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Extraordinarily long white pectoral fins that can be one-third the whale's body length - these 'wings' are often visible breaking the surface and are the most distinctive feature for identification.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Famous for breaching (launching completely out of water), tail slapping, and rolling at the surface. Often approaches boats curiously and may 'spy hop' by poking their heads vertically above water.

idTips.label: Throat & Belly
idTips.description: Deep grooves called pleats run from chin to belly, expanding like an accordion when feeding. The throat often appears white or light-colored with barnacle patches that feel rough and crusty.

idTips.label: Tail Fluke
idTips.description: Massive tail fluke with unique black and white patterns on the underside - each whale's pattern is like a fingerprint. Often raises tail high when diving, showing distinctive scalloped edges.

habitat: Humpback whales visit New England's coastal waters, particularly around Stellwagen Bank, Cape Cod Bay, and the Gulf of Maine during their feeding season. They prefer nutrient-rich waters where cold currents meet, creating ideal conditions for krill and small schooling fish. Look for them in areas 100-600 feet deep where underwater banks and ledges concentrate their prey.

seasonality.spring: Humpbacks begin arriving in New England waters as they migrate north from breeding grounds. Early arrivals may be seen in April, often appearing thin after their long journey without feeding.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for humpback viewing with the largest numbers present from June through September. Whales are actively feeding, making this the best time to witness bubble feeding and surface behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Whales continue feeding heavily through October and November, building up fat reserves for their southern migration. Many begin departing for breeding grounds by late fall.
seasonality.winter: Very few humpbacks remain in New England waters during winter months as most migrate to warmer breeding areas near the equator. Occasional stragglers may be spotted on warm winter days.

funFact: Humpback whales blow 'bubble nets' to catch their dinner - they swim in spirals underwater while releasing streams of bubbles that create a cylindrical net around schools of fish, then rocket up through the center with their mouths wide open, sometimes with several whales working together in this incredible feeding strategy.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with fin whales, but humpbacks have much longer pectoral fins, more tubercles on the head, and are much more acrobatic - if you see a whale breaching or tail slapping, it's almost certainly a humpback. Fin whales are sleeker, faster, and rarely show their tails when diving.
contextualKnowledge: Humpback whales were hunted nearly to extinction with populations dropping to just 5,000 individuals by the 1960s, but conservation efforts have helped them recover to about 135,000 worldwide. Each whale can be individually identified by the unique pattern on the underside of its tail fluke, and many whales that visit New England waters have been tracked and named by researchers for decades.
compareHints: Humpback whales are the only species in their genus Megaptera, making them unique among the rorqual family. Compared to other rorquals like fin whales and minke whales, humpbacks have proportionally much longer pectoral fins, more prominent tubercles on their heads, and are far more acrobatic in their surface behaviors. While other rorquals are built for speed and efficiency, humpbacks are the performers of the whale world.
